articles.title: Economics Nobel awarded for work on stabilizing economies in crisis
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03251-4Laureates share award that builds on the theories that contributed to governments intervening during the COVID-19 pandemic.
articles.content:
Credit: Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP via Getty

The 2026 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel has been awarded to economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford for their research on how to stabilize an economy to avoid socially and economically damaging fluctuations in inflation, growth and employment.

The work, in the words of the prize awarding committee, “generated a paradigm shift in stabilisation policy and [is] now used by central banks and finance ministries around the world”.

“This is an excellent prize, honouring two superb and highly influential economists,” says economist John Cochrane of the Hoover Institution, a thinktank based at Stanford University. Olivier Blanchard, formerly chief economist at the International Monetary Fund, says the laureates have “dramatically changed the conduct of monetary policy”.

According to Cochrane, there were “a dozen plausible contenders at least” to share a prize in this field. “I would hate to be the Nobel Prize committee deciding which two or three to recognize”, he says, but “Hall and Woodford were top contenders on anyone’s list”.

Speaking by phone during the prize announcement, Woodford said he was “elated” by the award. He added that his theory was intended not just to guide policy but also to help governments explain to the public why they make economic interventions in the way they do, “to talk to people about why the things that are being done are being done”.

“Together, Hall’s and Woodford’s contributions amount to a new foundation for the theory of macroeconomic fluctuations,” says the Nobel committee, “allowing us to obtain a deeper understanding of the sources and propagation mechanisms behind recessions and booms.”

The return of Keynes

The work of the two laureates, who share the prize of 12 million Swedish kronor (around US$1.2 million), builds on the ideas of the twentieth-century British economist John Maynard Keynes.

Credit: Tim Gidal/Picture Post/Hulton Archive/Getty

Keynes argued that governments need to intervene on a big scale in times of economic instability to avoid crashes and mass unemployment as happened in the Great Depression of the 1930s. Market forces alone cannot give an economy sufficient agility to respond to such crises, he contended in books such as How to Pay for the War (Macmillan, 1940), published just after Britain had declared war against Nazi Germany.

Keynes’ ideas became highly influential from the mid-twentieth-century onwards. They were relevant as recently as the COVID-19 pandemic when governments around the world funded businesses so they could retain their staff during lockdowns. But these ideas did not prevent the rollercoaster of economic boom and bust, evident for example in the oil crisis of the 1970s, and the financial crisis of 2008.

Hall and Woodford effect

Hall and Woodford’s work has helped to explain what was missing in Keynes’ macroeconomic picture — the study of the economy as a whole — by diving deep into the microeconomic perspective, which considers how decisions made by individual businesses and households affect prices, earnings and spending.

Hall, based at Stanford University in California, recognized that people’s decisions about consumption depend not just on quantifiable factors such as earnings but on what Keynes himself called “animal spirits”: psychological factors that drive economic choices, in this case expectations about the future.

In two key papers, in 1978 and in 1982, Hall showed that it is possible to estimate the proportion of spenders who take a rational view of how they think future monetary and fiscal policies might change, as well as those who in contrast make their decisions about consumption based only on an immediate, gloomy prospect of having no savings or access to borrowing. In effect, this amounts to estimating the proportions of the population that are forward-looking in their spending decisions and that are not. Hall validated his predictions against real-world data on consumption.

Woodford, based at Columbia University in New York, built on such work about expectations to create a 'New Keynesian' microeconomic theory, which culminated in his book Interest and Prices: Foundations of a Theory of Monetary Policy (Princeton University Press, 2003).
articles.reasoning: The article reports on the Nobel Prize awarded to economists whose research has fundamentally improved understanding and practice of economic stabilization policies. Their work has broad societal impact by helping governments better manage economic crises, reducing harmful fluctuations in inflation, growth, and employment, thereby improving quality of life globally. The article provides substantial context on their contributions and significance.
articles.personality_title: Nobel Prize honors economists who improved ways to steady troubled economies
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Economies can face sudden problems like rising prices, slow growth, or job losses. For many years, experts have studied how governments can help keep economies steady during these hard times. The ideas started by economist John Maynard Keynes in the 1900s showed that governments need to act during crises, but there were still questions about how to do this best.

**What happened** – In 2026, the Nobel Prize in Economics was awarded to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford for their important research on stabilizing economies. Their work explains how people’s spending choices and expectations about the future affect the economy. Hall studied how some people plan ahead while others focus only on their current money situation. Woodford built a new economic theory that helps central banks decide the best policies to keep inflation and unemployment under control.

**Impact** – Their research has changed how governments and central banks around the world manage economic crises. It helps avoid big swings in prices, growth, and jobs that can harm many people. For example, their ideas influenced actions taken during the COVID-19 pandemic when governments supported businesses to keep workers employed. This makes their work very important because it improves how economies recover from shocks.

**What's next step** – Governments and financial institutions will continue using Hall and Woodford’s theories to guide their decisions during future economic challenges. Their work also encourages further research to better understand how people’s choices affect the whole economy, possibly leading to even smarter policies.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford won the 2026 Nobel Prize for research that helps governments better stabilize economies by understanding how people’s spending decisions influence inflation, growth, and jobs.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le prix Nobel récompense des économistes qui ont amélioré la stabilité des économies en crise
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les économies peuvent connaître des problèmes soudains comme la hausse des prix, un ralentissement de la croissance ou la perte d’emplois. Depuis longtemps, les experts étudient comment les gouvernements peuvent aider à maintenir la stabilité en période difficile. Les idées de l’économiste John Maynard Keynes au XXe siècle ont montré que les gouvernements doivent agir en cas de crise, mais il restait des questions sur la meilleure façon de le faire.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – En 2026, le prix Nobel d’économie a été attribué à Robert E. Hall et Michael Woodford pour leurs recherches importantes sur la stabilisation des économies. Leur travail explique comment les choix de dépenses des personnes et leurs attentes sur l’avenir influencent l’économie. Hall a étudié comment certaines personnes planifient à l’avance tandis que d’autres se concentrent seulement sur leur situation financière actuelle. Woodford a développé une nouvelle théorie économique qui aide les banques centrales à décider des meilleures politiques pour contrôler l’inflation et le chômage.

**Impact** – Leurs recherches ont changé la manière dont les gouvernements et les banques centrales dans le monde gèrent les crises économiques. Elles aident à éviter de fortes fluctuations des prix, de la croissance et de l’emploi qui peuvent nuire à beaucoup de personnes. Par exemple, leurs idées ont influencé les mesures prises pendant la pandémie de COVID-19, lorsque les gouvernements ont soutenu les entreprises pour maintenir l’emploi. Leur travail est donc très important car il améliore la reprise économique après les chocs.

**Prochaine étape** – Les gouvernements et les institutions financières continueront d’utiliser les théories de Hall et Woodford pour guider leurs décisions lors de futures difficultés économiques. Leur travail encourage aussi de nouvelles recherches pour mieux comprendre comment les choix des individus affectent l’économie globale, ce qui pourrait conduire à des politiques encore plus efficaces.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Robert E. Hall et Michael Woodford ont reçu le prix Nobel 2026 pour des recherches qui aident les gouvernements à mieux stabiliser les économies en comprenant comment les décisions de dépenses influencent l’inflation, la croissance et l’emploi.

articles.title: What African elections can learn from the Borana Gadaa system
articles.summary: Discover how the Borana Gadaa system can inspire African elections through peaceful power transitions, accountable leadership, inclusive governance, and traditional democratic practices that strengthen public trust and participation.
articles.content:
This article by Diba Kosi Bilinga was originally published by Peace News Network on July 20, 2026. An edited version is being republished on Global Voices under a content partnership agreement.

Every election season, much of Africa braces itself. In some cases, incumbents amend constitutions to erase term limits, and citizens wait to see whether power will change hands at the ballot box or in the streets. The pattern repeats: disputed results, ethnic mobilization, coups, or leaders who refuse to leave.

Yet in the rangelands of southern Ethiopia and northern Kenya, the Borana Oromo people have long practiced rotational, peacefully transferred leadership. Known as the Borana Gadaa system, UNESCO inscribed it in 2016 as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity that regulates political and social life, resolves conflict, and protects women’s rights.

This article asks a question: What can African leaders, electoral commissions, political parties, and citizens learn from a governance model that has quietly rotated power every eight years for generations, without coups, without third-term referenda, and without the bloodshed that so often accompanies modern African elections?

Lesson 1: Power must have a time limit

Borana leadership rotates on a fixed eight-year cycle among five Gogeessas (parties). Each governs for one Gadaa period, then hands over power, returning to the first after 40 years — a rotation built into the structure itself.

Compare this to Africa’s modern pattern. Human Rights Watch (HRW) director Ida Sawyer describes a “constitutional coup” pattern: leaders who cannot win re-election simply rewrite the laws to get their way. Cameroon’s Paul Biya erased term limits in 2008 and has ruled since 1982; Uganda’s Museveni scrapped his in 2005; Rwanda, Burundi, Togo, Djibouti, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have each amended their constitutions to extend a president’s tenure.

Gadaa’s lesson is structural: When a time limit is built into the system itself, rather than a leader’s promise, departure never has to be settled by force.

Lesson 2: Prepare leaders before giving them power

Gadaa systems treat leadership as something built over decades, not switched on by an election. Members pass through age-grades from childhood, absorbing law, custom, and ritual responsibility long before they are eligible to lead — knowledge oral historians formally transmit across generations.

Most African political systems do the opposite: Candidates are selected first, and asked whether they are fit to govern only afterward. Patronage, money, and ethnic arithmetic often outweigh demonstrated understanding of law or public finance, producing leaders who improvise governance while learning on the job.

The lesson for African parties and civic institutions: Build structured pipelines — in local councils, youth wings, and civil service — that expose future leaders to responsibility long before a national mandate.

Lesson 3: Peaceful transitions are a sign of institutional strength, not weakness

Under the Gadaa system, at the Balli Walirafudhu handover ceremony, authority passes from the outgoing ruling class to the incoming one, understood by the whole community as final and binding. Every eight years, the Gumi Gaayo assembly, held under the sacred Odaa tree, reviews the era’s laws and blesses the incoming leadership.

Contrast that with Kenya’s 2007 to 08 crisis, when a disputed result triggered ethnic violence that killed roughly 1,000 people and displaced 500,000, per HRW’s investigation. Ivory Coast saw a similar rupture in 2010 to 2011, leading to a civil war.

In the Borana Gadaa system, succession is scripted years in advance. In much of Africa, it is an open question resolved only after votes are contested.

Lesson 4: No clan or ethnicity should own the political system

The Borana society has two broad blocks, the Sabboo Sadeen clan and the Goonaa Bal’aa clan, each with its own sub-clans. But the five Gogeessa that hold political authority cut across these clan lines — political identity and clan identity stay separate, so no single clan can capture the system.

This fault line has broken many African elections. The violence in Kenya in 2007 to 2008 was driven largely by ethnic mobilization, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) noting ethnicity as the main axis political elites mobilize around — turning elections into an ethnic census.

Where political identity is inseparable from ethnicity, losing an election can feel like losing everything for a whole community. Gadaa’s design offers a template: build structures — party membership, constituencies, civil-service recruitment — that mix identities rather than reinforce them.

Lesson 5: Democracy is more than voting day

Gadaa’s Gumi Gaayo assembly does far more than confirm who leads. It reviews the era’s laws, arbitrates disputes, and holds outgoing leaders publicly accountable — through consultation among elders and councils of advisors (Hayyuu), not a ballot cast once every few years.

Much of Africa’s politics concentrates almost all democratic energy into a single day. ITUC-Africa cataloged disputed results across Guinea, Togo, Sudan, Burundi, Burkina Faso, Egypt, Comoros, Tanzania, and Rwanda in 2010 alone — accountability between elections proved far weaker than the contest itself.

Robust democracies need standing institutions — independent courts, electoral commissions, a free press and community dispute-resolution bodies — that keep working every day of the cycle.

Lesson 6: Leadership should serve the institution, not the other way around

The Abbaa Gadaa — the topmost Borana Leader — never rules alone. He operates alongside the Hayyuu council of advisors, the Abbaa Seera responsible for law, and the ritual authority of the Qaalluu — a deliberately decentralized structure, as one account puts it, designed to stop any office from concentrating too much power.

Across Africa, the opposite dominates. A 2026 survey found rulers such as Cameroon’s Paul Biya (in power since 1982), Equatorial Guinea’s Teodoro Obiang Nguema Obiang (since 1979) and Congo’s Sassou Nguesso (since 1979) have systematically dismantled the checks meant to constrain them. In each case, the presidency grew larger than the constitution meant to contain it.

When power is distributed across councils, courts, and customary bodies, no single leader’s ambition can capture the whole state.

Lesson 7: Resolve conflict through dialogue before It becomes violence

Borana layers its conflict resolution: The Kora Gossa handles local clan disputes, the Gumi Gaayo settles national matters, and Boran Haraamu Koo’puu Rules — a form of social exclusion — is reserved for those who break the community’s deepest trust.

Modern West Africa shows what happens when such mediation is absent. Since 2020, the Sahel has seen a wave of takeovers — Mali, Guinea, Burkina Faso, Niger, Gabon — linked to deteriorating security and falling accountability in the years before each coup.

The lesson is not that customary courts should replace constitutions, but that no state can survive on election-day mechanisms alone — it needs everyday channels of mediation to build citizens’ trust.

Lesson 8: Culture, memory, and inclusion are part of governance

Borana Gadaa’s institutions are inseparable from Borana culture. The Odaa tree is both a meeting place and a living symbol of continuity across generations. Knowledge of the system’s history — including a documented line of more than 72 Abbaa Gadaa — is preserved and transmitted by oral historians.

Governance needs more than law and procedure — it needs cultural memory, shared symbols, and inclusive channels through which groups historically shut out of power, especially women, can still be heard.

African leaders don’t need to build Odaa trees or revive age-grade systems to learn from the Borana Gadaa. They need its underlying logic: time limits built into institutions, leaders prepared long before office, structures that cut across ethnic lines, power distributed across bodies, and dialogue running continuously rather than waiting for crisis.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights the Borana Gadaa system as an inspiring traditional governance model that promotes peaceful power transitions, accountable leadership, inclusive governance, and conflict resolution. These lessons offer meaningful, broad societal benefits for African elections and democratic practices, addressing significant challenges like election violence and authoritarianism. The detailed explanation of the system's principles provides substantial context and actionable insights for improving governance and democracy across Africa.
articles.personality_title: The Borana Gadaa system offers lessons for peaceful and fair African elections
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many African countries face repeated election problems, including leaders refusing to step down, violence, and ethnic conflicts. These issues often arise because of weak rules about power limits and poor leadership preparation.

**What happened** – The Borana Oromo people from southern Ethiopia and northern Kenya have a traditional system called the Borana Gadaa. This system peacefully rotates leadership every eight years among five groups, with clear rules and ceremonies that everyone respects. It has worked for generations without violence or power grabs.

**Impact** – The Borana Gadaa system shows how fixed time limits on leadership, careful training of future leaders, and mixing political power across clans can prevent many problems seen in modern African elections. It also uses regular meetings to review laws and hold leaders accountable, not just voting once every few years. This creates trust and stability.

**What's next step** – African countries can study and adapt the Borana Gadaa principles by building strong institutions that prepare leaders early, separate politics from ethnic identity, and maintain ongoing dialogue to solve conflicts peacefully. This could help reduce election violence and improve democracy.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The Borana Gadaa system teaches that peaceful, fair leadership changes happen when power is limited, leaders are prepared, and communities work together beyond election day.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le système Borana Gadaa offre des leçons pour des élections africaines pacifiques et équitables
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – De nombreux pays africains rencontrent des problèmes lors des élections, comme des dirigeants qui refusent de partir, des violences et des conflits ethniques. Ces problèmes viennent souvent de règles faibles sur les limites du pouvoir et d’un mauvais apprentissage des dirigeants.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le peuple Borana Oromo, dans le sud de l’Éthiopie et le nord du Kenya, a un système traditionnel appelé Borana Gadaa. Ce système fait tourner le pouvoir tous les huit ans entre cinq groupes, avec des règles claires et des cérémonies respectées par tous. Cela fonctionne depuis des générations sans violence ni prises de pouvoir illégales.

**Impact** – Le système Borana Gadaa montre comment des limites fixes au pouvoir, la formation soigneuse des futurs dirigeants et la répartition du pouvoir entre clans peuvent éviter beaucoup de problèmes des élections modernes en Afrique. Il utilise aussi des réunions régulières pour revoir les lois et contrôler les dirigeants, pas seulement un vote tous les quelques années. Cela crée confiance et stabilité.

**Prochaine étape** – Les pays africains peuvent étudier et adapter les principes du Borana Gadaa en construisant des institutions fortes qui préparent tôt les dirigeants, séparent politique et identité ethnique, et maintiennent un dialogue continu pour résoudre pacifiquement les conflits. Cela pourrait réduire les violences électorales et améliorer la démocratie.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Le système Borana Gadaa montre que des changements de pouvoir pacifiques et justes arrivent quand le pouvoir est limité, les dirigeants préparés, et les communautés unies au-delà du jour des élections.
articles.personality_title_es: El sistema Borana Gadaa ofrece lecciones para elecciones africanas pacíficas y justas
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Muchos países africanos enfrentan problemas en las elecciones, como líderes que no quieren dejar el poder, violencia y conflictos étnicos. Estos problemas suelen ocurrir por reglas débiles sobre límites de poder y falta de preparación de los líderes.

**Qué pasó** – El pueblo Borana Oromo, en el sur de Etiopía y norte de Kenia, tiene un sistema tradicional llamado Borana Gadaa. Este sistema rota el liderazgo cada ocho años entre cinco grupos, con reglas claras y ceremonias que todos respetan. Ha funcionado por generaciones sin violencia ni golpes de estado.

**Impacto** – El sistema Borana Gadaa muestra cómo los límites fijos al poder, la formación cuidadosa de futuros líderes y la mezcla del poder entre clanes pueden evitar muchos problemas de las elecciones modernas en África. También usa reuniones regulares para revisar leyes y controlar a los líderes, no solo votar cada pocos años. Esto crea confianza y estabilidad.

**Próximo paso** – Los países africanos pueden estudiar y adaptar los principios del Borana Gadaa construyendo instituciones fuertes que preparen líderes temprano, separen la política de la identidad étnica y mantengan un diálogo continuo para resolver conflictos pacíficamente. Esto podría reducir la violencia electoral y mejorar la democracia.

**Resumen en una frase** – El sistema Borana Gadaa enseña que los cambios de poder pacíficos y justos ocurren cuando el poder tiene límites, los líderes están preparados y las comunidades trabajan juntas más allá del día de las elecciones.

articles.title: Colombia peace deal must endure as insecurity grows, Security Council hears
articles.summary: Nearly 10 years after Colombia signed a historic peace agreement to end a decades-long insurgency, the deal is under strain from growing insecurity – and the UN’s top official in the country says it cannot be allowed to falter.
articles.content:
Miroslav Jenča told the Security Council on Monday that the 2016 accord must be implemented in full, with proper funding, better coordination between institutions and protection for former combatants.

He pointed to real gains: rural development, and mechanisms for transitional justice and reparation for victims. But he admitted that implementation has had “many shortcomings” and that much remains to be done.

Security policy and the peace agreement should reinforce each other, Mr. Jenča said, and the accord should be carried out comprehensively.

“We look forward to the further definition of its policies, and we stand ready to support the Government in this regard,” he said, offering the experience gained by the UN Verification Mission over almost a decade of supporting implementation.

Violence stalks communities

Communities in conflict-affected regions remain exposed to armed groups, geographical isolation and limited access to public services. Child recruitment, particularly among ethnic communities, and threats and attacks against women remain major concerns, ambassadors heard.

Tweet URL

Government data presented to legislators show that illegal armed groups grew from around 15,000 members in 2022 to approximately 28,000 today.

Mr. Jenča also condemned the killings of civil society leaders María Ovidia Palechor and James Flor in Cauca on 1 September, highlighting the risks faced by rights defenders.

He said expanding economic opportunities, improving public services and strengthening local institutions were essential to reducing violence.

Reintegration commitment

Despite these challenges, more than 11,000 former members of the FARC-EP rebel group remain committed to reintegration.

With State and international support, they have developed around 6,000 productive projects and 300 cooperatives in sectors including agriculture, tourism, trade and textiles.

Mr. Jenča highlighted tourism initiatives involving former combatants and victims, aimed at stimulating local economies and job markets.

However, economic sustainability and security remain significant challenges. Since the agreement was signed in 2016, 501 former combatants have been killed, most recently on 22 September in Cesar.

The Special Representative reaffirmed the UN mission's readiness to continue supporting implementation and highlighted its value on the ground, noting that over almost a decade it had built relationships of trust in some of regions most impacted by continuing violence.

Colombia had entered “a new political chapter, with wide ranging challenges ahead,” Mr. Jenča said, calling for “sustained international engagement in order to overcome remaining obstacles.”

articles.personality_title: Colombia’s peace deal shows progress amid security challenges
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In 2016, Colombia signed a peace agreement to end a long conflict with the FARC-EP rebel group. Nearly 10 years later, the country still faces violence and insecurity, but efforts to keep the peace deal alive continue.

**What happened** – On September 25, 2023, Miroslav Jenča, the UN’s top official in Colombia, spoke to the Security Council about the importance of fully carrying out the peace agreement. He explained that while there have been problems, there is real progress in rural development, justice for victims, and helping former rebels start new lives. However, violence and threats against communities, especially women and children, remain serious issues.

**Impact** – The peace deal is important because it supports rebuilding areas hurt by years of fighting. More than 11,000 former rebels are working on about 6,000 projects like farming and tourism, which help local economies grow. Still, dangers remain, as many ex-combatants have been killed since the deal began. The UN mission has built trust in these regions and continues to help protect people and guide the peace process.

**What's next step** – The Colombian government, with help from the UN and other partners, plans to improve funding, coordinate better between agencies, and protect vulnerable groups. They also want to expand economic chances and public services to reduce violence. Continued international support will be key to overcoming challenges and making the peace deal last.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Colombia’s peace agreement faces challenges but shows important progress through community projects and ongoing UN support to build a safer future.
articles.personality_title_fr: L’accord de paix en Colombie progresse malgré les défis sécuritaires
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – En 2016, la Colombie a signé un accord de paix pour mettre fin à un long conflit avec le groupe rebelle FARC-EP. Près de 10 ans plus tard, le pays fait encore face à la violence, mais les efforts pour maintenir l’accord de paix se poursuivent.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le 25 septembre 2023, Miroslav Jenča, le principal responsable de l’ONU en Colombie, a parlé au Conseil de sécurité de l’importance de mettre pleinement en œuvre l’accord de paix. Il a expliqué que malgré des difficultés, des progrès réels ont été réalisés dans le développement rural, la justice pour les victimes et l’aide aux anciens rebelles pour commencer une nouvelle vie. Cependant, la violence et les menaces contre les communautés, notamment les femmes et les enfants, restent des problèmes sérieux.

**Impact** – L’accord de paix est important car il soutient la reconstruction des zones touchées par des années de combats. Plus de 11 000 anciens rebelles travaillent sur environ 6 000 projets comme l’agriculture et le tourisme, ce qui aide à développer les économies locales. Pourtant, les dangers persistent, car de nombreux ex-combattants ont été tués depuis le début de l’accord. La mission de l’ONU a construit la confiance dans ces régions et continue d’aider à protéger les populations et à guider le processus de paix.

**Prochaine étape** – Le gouvernement colombien, avec l’aide de l’ONU et d’autres partenaires, prévoit d’améliorer le financement, de mieux coordonner les agences et de protéger les groupes vulnérables. Il souhaite aussi élargir les opportunités économiques et les services publics pour réduire la violence. Un soutien international continu sera essentiel pour surmonter les défis et faire durer l’accord de paix.

**Résumé en une phrase** – L’accord de paix en Colombie rencontre des défis, mais montre des progrès importants grâce aux projets communautaires et au soutien continu de l’ONU pour construire un avenir plus sûr.
articles.personality_title_es: El acuerdo de paz en Colombia avanza pese a desafíos de seguridad
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En 2016, Colombia firmó un acuerdo de paz para terminar un largo conflicto con el grupo rebelde FARC-EP. Casi 10 años después, el país aún enfrenta violencia, pero los esfuerzos para mantener el acuerdo continúan.

**Qué pasó** – El 25 de septiembre de 2023, Miroslav Jenča, el principal representante de la ONU en Colombia, habló ante el Consejo de Seguridad sobre la importancia de cumplir completamente el acuerdo de paz. Explicó que, aunque hay problemas, se han logrado avances reales en desarrollo rural, justicia para las víctimas y ayuda a exrebeldes para empezar nuevas vidas. Sin embargo, la violencia y las amenazas contra comunidades, especialmente mujeres y niños, siguen siendo preocupaciones importantes.

**Impacto** – El acuerdo de paz es importante porque ayuda a reconstruir zonas afectadas por años de conflicto. Más de 11,000 exrebeldes trabajan en unos 6,000 proyectos como agricultura y turismo, que impulsan las economías locales. Aún así, persisten los peligros, ya que muchos excombatientes han sido asesinados desde que comenzó el acuerdo. La misión de la ONU ha construido confianza en estas regiones y sigue ayudando a proteger a las personas y a guiar el proceso de paz.

**Próximo paso** – El gobierno colombiano, con ayuda de la ONU y otros socios, planea mejorar la financiación, coordinar mejor las agencias y proteger a los grupos vulnerables. También quieren ampliar las oportunidades económicas y los servicios públicos para reducir la violencia. El apoyo internacional continuo será clave para superar los retos y hacer que el acuerdo de paz dure.

**Resumen en una frase** – El acuerdo de paz en Colombia enfrenta desafíos pero muestra avances importantes mediante proyectos comunitarios y apoyo constante de la ONU para construir un futuro más seguro.

articles.title: Poetry book promotes Chabacano, Asia’s only Spanish-based creole language
articles.summary: "The project highlights not only the continued vitality of Chavacano as a language, but also the efforts of its speakers to create new literature and preserve the language through writing.”
articles.content:
A new poetry anthology features writers of Chabacano, one of the Philippines’ 170 languages, which is widely spoken in the southernmost city of Zamboanga, and stands out as Asia’s only Spanish-based creole language.

The Philippines was a colony of Spain for more than three centuries, but the Spanish language was only used by the elite, friars, and colonial rulers. Only in Zamboanga did a Spanish-based creole language develop.

In 2018, Global Voices featured Bien Chabacano, a blog dedicated to promoting and documenting Chavacano de Zamboanga. Its creator, Jerome Herrera, launched a book project this year by inviting writers to submit poems to be compiled in an anthology. This led to the launch of the “Sombra y Luz” book in July, featuring 23 poems by 10 authors. The poems are mainly about love, family, and Zamboangueño identity.

Herrera said, “The project highlights not only the continued vitality of Chavacano as a literary language, but also the efforts of its speakers to create new literature and preserve the language through writing.”

He added that the book title aims to convey a message of contrast about the changes in Zamboanga City. The book cover also provides a nostalgic reference to the flowers that decorated the city in the past.

The cover features an American-era style lamppost that can be seen along the Zamboanga boulevard. The cover also features bougainvilleas which my dad tells me were ubiquitous in Zamboanga City back when it was known as the Ciudad de Flores.

Herrera’s poem in the anthology mentions flowers and birds that enrich life in the city.

Maga pajaro que ta vola-vola,

Na maga rama de pono ta queda,

Alegre con uno y otro ta grita-grita,

Twit! Twit! Twit! Entero el dia. Mio pueblo Ciudad de Zamboanga,

Ciudad de Flores que llama.

De noche mucho pajaro ay columbra,

Na maga cable de corriente ta esta.

Birds that fly and flutter freely,

Perched upon the branches of trees,

Singing and calling each other joyfully,

Tweet! Tweet! Tweet! All day long. Oh, my beloved City of Zamboanga,

City of Flowers, they call you.

At night, many birds can be found,

Sitting on wires, that’s what they do.

In an interview with Global Voices, Herrera noted the heavy use of Spanish words in the selected poems:

…there is a lot of debate with regards to what Chabacano poetry should look like. For some, they like it with a lot of Spanish words and for others, they like it to be exactly as how Chabacano appears in everyday conversations. Most of the poems submitted leaned heavily on Spanish words, I think primarily because Chabacano writers rely on Spanish words to make their works sound more formal as well as more poetic. Since it’s poetry, I thought that it was alright to present Chabacano in an idealistic manner.

He added that the anthology seeks to encourage more people to accept the various ways that Chabacano is used.

For a very long time, people have been putting Chabacano inside a box. I hope that these books open up conversations regarding Chabacano literature and make people receptive to different kinds of writing styles in Chabacano.

This approach is evident in the poem “Escribi Chavacano, Conversa Chabacano,” which celebrates Chabacano as a living language.

Through references to poems, essays, fables, and the stories passed down by elders, the author reminds readers that the language continues to thrive when it is written, spoken, and shared with others. The title itself is noteworthy for its use of both Chavacano and Chabacano, reflecting the coexistence of two accepted spellings of the language. In doing so, the poem highlights not only the importance of preserving Chabacano, but also the richness and diversity of its written tradition.

Herrera’s interview with Asymptote Journal noted the challenge of finding Chabacano contributors, and his hope that the book project can lead to more literary initiatives.

articles.personality_title: New poetry book celebrates Chabacano, Asia’s unique Spanish-based language
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Chabacano is a special language spoken in Zamboanga City in the Philippines. It is Asia’s only Spanish-based creole language, which means it mixes Spanish with local languages. While the Philippines was ruled by Spain for over 300 years, Chabacano is the only language in the region that grew from Spanish and is still used today.

**What happened** – A new poetry book called “Sombra y Luz” was released in July. It features 23 poems by 10 writers who use Chabacano. The poems talk about love, family, and life in Zamboanga. The book was created by Jerome Herrera, who started a blog to promote Chabacano and invited writers to submit their work for this collection.

**Impact** – This book is important because it shows that Chabacano is still a living language with people who want to write and create new stories in it. It helps keep the language alive and encourages others to accept different ways of using Chabacano, especially in poetry. The book also connects readers to the culture and history of Zamboanga through its words and images.

**What’s next step** – Jerome Herrera hopes this anthology will inspire more writers to create Chabacano literature. He wants it to open conversations about the language and lead to more projects that celebrate and preserve Chabacano.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new poetry collection shines a light on Chabacano, supporting the survival and growth of Asia’s only Spanish-based creole language through literature.
